analysis.one_liner: Makes deploying a national missile defense shield official United States policy.
analysis.headline: Backed by 28 Republican cosponsors and a favorable Senate committee report, the bill still never received a Senate vote before the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it U.S. policy to build and deploy a nationwide missile defense system capable of stopping a limited ballistic missile attack, with an initial capability deadline of the end of 2003. It orders the Pentagon to develop interceptors, ground-based radars, space-based sensors, and battle-management systems, run an end-to-end test by the end of fiscal 1999, and report to Congress on the costs for fiscal 1998 through 2003. Because deployment would conflict with the 1972 ABM Treaty with Russia, it urges renegotiation and directs the President and Congress to consider withdrawing from the treaty if no agreement is reached within a year. The Senate Armed Services Committee approved it, but the full Senate never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: The immediate beneficiaries are the contractors who would build the system: interceptor makers, radar and space-sensor manufacturers, and battle-management developers, who would receive a legally mandated, deadline-driven development and procurement program with streamlined acquisition rules. Supporters also claimed a public benefit: protection for the entire country against a limited missile attack, including an accidental or unauthorized launch.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Missile defense contractors; Americans if the shield works

how_it_helps.text: Makes deployment of a defense of the whole country against limited ballistic missile attack — whether accidental, unauthorized, or deliberate — official U.S. policy, with an initial operational capability required by the end of 2003.

Directs the Secretary of Defense to develop the full system — interceptors, fixed ground radars, space-based sensors, and battle management, command, control, and communications — and to conduct an integrated systems test by the end of fiscal 1999.

Requires a report to Congress within 120 days of enactment covering the chosen architecture, the appropriations needed for fiscal 1998 through 2003, and the point at which the program would conflict with the ABM Treaty — a built-in public accounting of cost and treaty consequences.

Presses the President to negotiate changes to the ABM Treaty with Russia, requires any amendment to come to the Senate for approval, and sets a fallback: if no agreement is reached within a year, the President and Congress must consider withdrawing from the treaty.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers, through Defense Department appropriations for research, development, testing, and procurement in fiscal 1998-2003 — an amount the bill does not cap and instead requires the Pentagon to estimate after enactment. The bill also spreads risk more broadly: its own text anticipates a collision with the 1972 ABM Treaty and lays out a path toward U.S. withdrawal, which would end a cornerstone of the U.S.-Russian arms-control framework. The fixed 2003 deadline and streamlined acquisition procedures shift schedule pressure onto the program, with cost overruns and technical failure risks ultimately landing on taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a hard 2003 deployment deadline but sets no spending limit; it requires only an after-the-fact estimate of the appropriations needed for fiscal 1998 through 2003, committing Congress to a program whose total cost is unspecified.

The bill's own text concedes the program would eventually conflict with the 1972 ABM Treaty and requires the President and Congress to consider withdrawing from the treaty if Russia does not agree to amendments within a year — putting an established arms-control framework at risk to clear the way for deployment.

The schedule is out of order with the testing plan: the first full integrated systems test is required only by the end of fiscal 1999, while the deployment capability is mandated by the end of 2003, so the deadline would be locked in before the system had proven it could work.
The bill directs the Pentagon to use streamlined acquisition procedures to speed the program, reducing the standard oversight and competition checks that normally apply to major weapons development.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters had a real argument: in 1997 the United States relied entirely on offensive deterrence, and the bill's stated aim was to protect every American against a limited missile attack, including an accidental or unauthorized launch. But the bill's design favored the builders over the taxpayers: it fixed a deployment date before the technology had been tested end-to-end, left the price tag to a future estimate with no cap, and prescribed streamlined acquisition that trims oversight. It also treated abandoning the ABM Treaty as the default fallback. The assured winners were the contractors who would build the system; the promised protection depended on unproven technology, and the arms-control risk was real.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Armed Services Committee and sat on the Senate's waiting list for floor business for 20 months, but it was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Trent Lott, the Senate Majority Leader, introduced the bill on January 21, 1997 along with 25 Republican colleagues; 28 senators cosponsored it in total, all Republican.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which ordered it reported favorably without amendment on April 24, 1997 and reported it on April 30 with written report 105-15; additional and minority views were filed.
On April 30, 1997 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — Calendar No. 42 — the queue of bills waiting for floor time.
No further action was ever taken: the Senate never debated or voted on the bill, and it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers were never committed to the bill's uncapped costs or to its fallback of withdrawing from the ABM Treaty, and missile defense contractors lost the statutory mandate and fixed deadline this bill would have handed them. Supporters of a missile shield got nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, who never funded this mandate

for.name: Sen. Trent Lott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Strom Thurmond
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably out of committee without amendment and filed the written report.

against.name: Senate Armed Services Committee Democrats
against.role: Minority members of the reporting committee
against.what_they_did: Filed additional and minority views on the committee report rather than joining the favorable report.

against.name: Clinton administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed statutory deployment deadlines that would force changes to, or withdrawal from, the ABM Treaty.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors were Republicans and none of the 45 Senate Democrats signed on; the committee's favorable report nonetheless drew minority views, and the bill never reached the floor for a roll call.

industries.industry: Ballistic missile defense contractors (interceptors, radars, space sensors, battle management)
industries.note: The bill orders the Pentagon to develop and deploy the full system by a fixed 2003 date and to use streamlined acquisition procedures, turning development into a deadline-driven, multibillion-dollar contract stream paid for by taxpayers with no spending cap in the bill. At the time of the bill the technology had never been tested end-to-end, so the contractors' revenue was guaranteed while the public's protection was not.
